title: Can a knot match its mirror?
hook: Hold a rope trefoil up to a mirror. Can you ever make the rope match its reflection?

knows: what a mirror image is, and that a trefoil is a closed loop with three crossings
doesNotKnow: that turning a knot over is a way of moving it, so it never changes the knot, while its mirror image can be a different knot: no wiggling turns the left-handed trefoil into the right-handed one. The figure-eight is its own mirror image.

misconception: A mirror image is the same knot; you just flip it over.
objective: The learner can explain that turning the trefoil over leaves every crossing mark the same, so it is the same knot, while the mirror changes every mark, and that the trefoil cannot be moved into its mirror image.
keyState: Two milestones on the trefoil: 'turned' (card turned over at rest, on either side of the mirror: W-1606) and 'mirrored' (mirrored on either face, marks +,+,+, Sum +3). The seen line 'Trefoil: turned over −3 · mirror +3' is never cleared; its 'turned over' segment is written only from the plain turned state (unmirrored, marks −,−,−, Sum −3), its 'mirror' segment at the first mirrored rest. Optional, not on the QA path: 'eightMirror' (figure-eight mirrored, Sum 0).

claims.text: The trefoil is chiral: the left- and right-handed trefoils cannot be moved into each other; Max Dehn proved it in 1914 ('Mirroring turned every mark plus, and no wiggling gets back: the trefoil is not its own mirror image, as Max Dehn proved in 1914'; 'So a trefoil comes in a left and a right version'; predict answer 'No, never').

claims.text: Convention: a crossing mark is plus (right-handed) when the over-strand passes from left to right as seen travelling along the under-strand; a drawing whose marks sum below 0 is called left-handed and above 0 right-handed, and the table's trefoil is the left-handed one (stage 'Left-handed' / 'Right-handed', badges '+' / '−', 'Sum'; reveal 'its hand stayed left'; predict 'A left-handed trefoil and its mirror image, the right-handed one').

recall.question: You hold a right-handed trefoil made of rope. You turn it upside down and lay it flat. What do you have?
options: Either, depending on how you lay it
recall.why: Turning a knot over is a way of moving it, and moving never changes the knot. Only a mirror image swaps the trefoil's hand, and no move reaches it.
